name: N-acetylcysteine (NAC)
summary: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is a modified form of the amino acid cysteine. It is both a long-established medicine with specific medical uses and an ingredient sold in supplements; those uses should not be confused.
commonUses: May boost glutathione, the body's main antioxidant
May support lung health and thin mucus
May support liver health and detox
May improve hormones and ovulation in PCOS
roles: Supplies cysteine, a building block the body uses to make glutathione, its main internal antioxidant.
Its chemistry on mucus proteins is why it is used in mucus-thinning medicines; this is a medical use, not a general supplement benefit.

status.note: There is no routine test for NAC status and no NAC deficiency is defined.

low.note: NAC is not an essential nutrient. No deficiency condition or required intake has been established.

high.note: No safe upper amount is set for supplements. Side effects depend on the amount, the route (oral, inhaled, intravenous) and the person.

foodSources.note: Food contains ordinary cysteine as part of protein, not NAC. Eating protein is a different intervention from taking NAC.

forms.name: Oral supplements
forms.note: Capsules and powders. Their marketing is separate from the indications and supervision attached to medicines.

forms.name: Acetylcysteine medicines
forms.note: Oral, inhaled and intravenous medical products. Route and purpose matter; an oral supplement is not a substitute for emergency or prescribed treatment.

forms.name: Combination products (e.g. GlyNAC)
forms.note: NAC mixed with glycine or other ingredients. Findings about a mixture cannot be assigned to NAC alone.

reference.noUpperLimit: No tolerable upper intake level for N-acetylcysteine was found from EFSA or other official sources in the searches made for this guide. That is not proof that none exists, and not evidence that any amount is safe. Health Canada has licensing dose limits for some of these ingredients; they are product-licensing rules, not safety limits.

interactions.note: NAC can increase the blood-pressure-lowering effect of nitroglycerin. Discuss the combination with the prescribing clinician or pharmacist.
Supplement safety has not been established during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Discuss it with a doctor or pharmacist.

cautions: Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea can occur with NAC.
Acetylcysteine is used medically for paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning. Suspected poisoning needs urgent medical care, not self-treatment with a supplement.
Safety information for an intravenous or inhaled medicine cannot simply be applied to an oral supplement. This guide does not establish long-term supplement safety.

origin: NAC is made in a laboratory by adding an acetyl group to cysteine, an amino acid the body gets from protein. It has been used as a medicine for decades, for example for paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose and as a mucus thinner.
Supplement NAC is sold as capsules and powders. That marketing is separate from the supervised medical uses, and evidence from one use does not carry over to the other.
dosage: There is no established daily requirement or upper limit for supplements. Amounts in studies and products vary widely, and this guide does not set one.
An amount commonly used in studies and supplements is about 1,600 mg a day. This is not a reference intake or a personal recommendation.
Check the NAC content in milligrams (mg) on the label, and avoid combining several products that contain it. Combination products with glycine or vitamin C need their own label check.

foodAmounts.verdict: No. NAC is a modified form of cysteine made for medicines and supplements. Food contains ordinary cysteine inside proteins, not NAC, so there is no whole-food amount to compare with the 1,600 mg commonly used in supplements.
